title: Brigatinib Therapy
schedule_label: Continuous oral treatment with a seven-day lead-in
context_label: ALK-positive advanced NSCLC · before an ALK inhibitor or after crizotinib
scope_note: Brigatinib on its own for adults with ALK-positive advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: either after crizotinib (00562a) or before any ALK inhibitor (00562b). This is not an adjuvant course or a general pathway after every ALK inhibitor.
purpose: Brigatinib is a targeted medicine intended to control ALK-positive advanced lung cancer. The choice depends on the cancer’s ALK result, previous treatment, your health and your priorities.
indication_text: Brigatinib on its own for adults with ALK-positive advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: either after crizotinib (00562a) or before any ALK inhibitor (00562b). This is not an adjuvant course or a general pathway after every ALK inhibitor.
schedule_summary: The usual starting plan is 90 mg once daily for seven days, then 180 mg once daily if your team confirms the increase. Some people need a different dose. Treatment continues while helping and tolerable, with regular reviews and no fixed number of cycles.
administration_text: Swallow the tablets whole with water, with or without food. Do not crush, chew or split them. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice. If a dose is missed or you vomit after it, do not take an extra dose; take the next dose at its usual time. Contact the team for ongoing vomiting or difficulty keeping fluids or medicine down.
monitoring_summary: Before starting: ALK result, blood count, kidney/liver tests, breathing-function assessment, ECG, blood pressure, fasting glucose, muscle enzyme CPK and pancreatic enzymes. Review breathing symptoms on days 8 and 15, then monthly or sooner if needed. ECG and blood pressure are checked every two weeks initially, then monthly. Liver tests are every two weeks for the first three months, then as advised. Blood count, kidneys, fasting glucose, CPK and pancreatic enzymes are usually checked monthly. Scans follow your Consultant’s plan.

agents.name: Brigatinib
agents.mechanism: Blocks an abnormal ALK growth signal
agents.explanation: An altered ALK gene can drive cancer-cell growth. Brigatinib blocks the activity of this signal. Testing confirms whether this target is present; the medicine can also affect healthy tissues, so regular checks and early symptom reporting matter.
agents.watch: Report breathing changes immediately, especially in the first week. Follow the exact tablet strength and lead-in plan; check all new medicines with your pharmacist.
risks: Lung inflammation or early breathing reactions, which can be serious or fatal
Raised blood pressure or a slow heartbeat
Liver injury and abnormal liver tests
Raised muscle enzyme with muscle pain or weakness
Raised pancreatic enzymes; report severe abdominal pain
Diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, reduced appetite and fatigue
Skin rash and sensitivity to sunlight
Low blood counts and infection risk
Allergic reactions; pregnancy and fertility risks

phases_title: Lead-in, continuing tablets and regular reviews
phases_note: The usual starting plan is 90 mg once daily for seven days, then 180 mg once daily if your team confirms the increase. Some people need a different dose. Treatment continues while helping and tolerable, with regular reviews and no fixed number of cycles.
timeline_note: Relative treatment milestones, not equal time intervals or booked appointments. New symptoms can occur at any time.
safety_note: Report breathing changes immediately. A normal recent blood test does not make a new symptom safe to ignore.
teachback: Can you explain the seven-day lead-in, who authorises a dose increase or restart, what to do after a missed or vomited dose, which checks are due and how to get urgent help?
consent_support: Discuss the exact indication and prior ALK treatment, likely benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including not proceeding, serious lung/heart/liver/glucose/vision risks, common symptoms, fertility and contraception, monitoring and the practical tablet plan. Agree who reviews a hold or restart. Consent can be reconsidered.
urgent_extra: Contact your oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, cough or fever, especially during the first week but also later. Do not wait for a booked check. Urgent advice is also needed for fainting, a very slow heartbeat, chest pain, severe headache or vision changes, marked muscle pain/weakness, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, unusual thirst or frequent urination, jaundice or severe diarrhoea. Major breathing difficulty, collapse or severe chest pain needs emergency help.

chapters.title: Why brigatinib is being considered
chapters.intro: Confirm the cancer test and previous treatment before choosing this medicine.

items.title: Two distinct treatment settings
items.text: Brigatinib on its own for adults with ALK-positive advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: either after crizotinib (00562a) or before any ALK inhibitor (00562b). This is not an adjuvant course or a general pathway after every ALK inhibitor.

items.title: What the medicine does
items.text: An altered ALK gene can drive cancer-cell growth. Brigatinib blocks the activity of this signal. Testing confirms whether this target is present; the medicine can also affect healthy tissues, so regular checks and early symptom reporting matter.

items.title: How long treatment lasts
items.text: The usual starting plan is 90 mg once daily for seven days, then 180 mg once daily if your team confirms the increase. Some people need a different dose. Treatment continues while helping and tolerable, with regular reviews and no fixed number of cycles.

chapters.title: Taking treatment at home
chapters.intro: Your prescription is the individual plan.

items.title: Taking the tablets
items.text: Swallow the tablets whole with water, with or without food. Do not crush, chew or split them. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice. If a dose is missed or you vomit after it, do not take an extra dose; take the next dose at its usual time. Contact the team for ongoing vomiting or difficulty keeping fluids or medicine down.

items.title: Lead-in and dose increase
items.text: The usual starting plan is 90 mg once daily for seven days, then 180 mg once daily if your team confirms the increase. Some people need a different dose. Treatment continues while helping and tolerable, with regular reviews and no fixed number of cycles.

items.title: After a pause
items.text: Do not restart or increase brigatinib yourself. A break of 14 days or more for a reason other than a side effect normally needs a new seven-day lead-in before the previously tolerated dose. A break because of a side effect follows a different recovery plan. Early lung inflammation can prevent the usual increase to 180 mg.

items.title: Missed or vomited dose
items.text: Do not replace the dose or double the next dose. Resume at the next scheduled time and contact the team if symptoms prevent treatment.

chapters.title: Checks before and during treatment
chapters.intro: Some important reactions appear before the next appointment.

items.title: Baseline and ongoing checks
items.text: Before starting: ALK result, blood count, kidney/liver tests, breathing-function assessment, ECG, blood pressure, fasting glucose, muscle enzyme CPK and pancreatic enzymes. Review breathing symptoms on days 8 and 15, then monthly or sooner if needed. ECG and blood pressure are checked every two weeks initially, then monthly. Liver tests are every two weeks for the first three months, then as advised. Blood count, kidneys, fasting glucose, CPK and pancreatic enzymes are usually checked monthly. Scans follow your Consultant’s plan.

items.title: Breathing needs particular attention
items.text: Most early pulmonary reactions happen in the first seven days, but lung inflammation can occur later. Report new cough, breathlessness or fever straight away; the team may pause treatment while checking the cause.

items.title: Muscles, pancreas and glucose
items.text: Blood tests can identify changes before symptoms. Report muscle pain or weakness, severe abdominal pain, unusual thirst or frequent urination.

chapters.title: Other medicines, skin and family planning
chapters.intro: Ask before changing other medicines or the brigatinib dose.

items.title: Interaction review
items.text: Some antibiotics, antifungals, antivirals, seizure medicines and herbal products can alter treatment. Your oncology pharmacist must review the complete medicine list. Do not change existing medicines yourself.

items.title: Sun protection
items.text: Avoid prolonged sun exposure during treatment and for at least five days afterwards. Use protective clothing, a hat, broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher sunscreen and lip balm. Report severe rash or sun reaction.

items.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
items.text: Discuss fertility before treatment. Effective non-hormonal contraception is advised for women during treatment and for at least four months after the last dose; men with partners who could become pregnant need effective contraception during treatment and for at least three months afterwards. Tell the team promptly about possible pregnancy. Breastfeeding must stop during treatment.

items.title: Driving and daily tasks
items.text: Blurred vision, dizziness or fatigue can affect driving and machinery. Avoid these activities when affected and discuss persistent symptoms.

chapters.title: When to seek help
chapters.intro: Follow your treating hospital’s urgent-contact instructions.

items.title: Call promptly
items.text: Contact your oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, cough or fever, especially during the first week but also later. Do not wait for a booked check. Urgent advice is also needed for fainting, a very slow heartbeat, chest pain, severe headache or vision changes, marked muscle pain/weakness, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, unusual thirst or frequent urination, jaundice or severe diarrhoea. Major breathing difficulty, collapse or severe chest pain needs emergency help.

items.title: When you call
items.text: Give the medicine, current dose, when symptoms started and when the last dose was taken. Say whether you can drink, pass urine and manage daily activities; do not delay calling to collect details.

support.title: One written tablet plan
support.text: Keep the current dose, tablet strengths and next review clear. Ask the pharmacist about safe storage, handling and returning unused tablets. Do not share medicines.

support.title: Anti-sickness medicines only if needed
support.text: Brigatinib has minimal-to-low oral sickness risk. The oral NCCP guidance uses anti-sickness medicines as required; your team chooses a suitable medicine, dose and duration. Persistent vomiting still needs advice.

support.title: Food and other medicines
support.text: Take with or without food; avoid grapefruit. Check every prescription, herbal or non-prescription product, including St John’s wort, before starting or stopping it.

support.title: Skin and sunshine
support.text: Avoid prolonged sun exposure during treatment and for at least five days afterwards. Use protective clothing, a hat, broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher sunscreen and lip balm. Report severe rash or sun reaction.

support.title: Symptoms and practical support
support.text: Keep the 24-hour oncology contact available. Ask early for help with symptoms, eating, tablet supply, work, travel or emotional wellbeing.

evidence.title: Why this ALK-targeted medicine may be chosen
evidence.intro: Clinical studies support brigatinib in selected ALK-positive advanced lung cancers before any ALK inhibitor and after crizotinib. The studies involved different treatment settings.
evidence.population: Adults with ALK-positive advanced NSCLC, separated by previous ALK treatment
evidence.interpretation: The medicine can control cancer in appropriately selected people. Your team assesses benefit with symptoms, scans and regular review.
evidence.limitations: Trial averages cannot predict your outcome or establish which modern ALK inhibitor is best for you. Discuss your treatment choices and priorities.

chronology_notes.title: Before treatment
chronology_notes.text: Confirm ALK and prior treatment, baseline tests, dose, interactions and contacts.

chronology_notes.title: First seven days
chronology_notes.text: Usual 90 mg daily lead-in, with close attention to new respiratory symptoms.

chronology_notes.title: Day eight and beyond
chronology_notes.text: Only increase when authorised; usual ongoing dose is 180 mg daily. Day 8 and 15 pulmonary reviews do not replace urgent reporting.

chronology_notes.title: After a pause
chronology_notes.text: Do not restart or increase brigatinib yourself. A break of 14 days or more for a reason other than a side effect normally needs a new seven-day lead-in before the previously tolerated dose. A break because of a side effect follows a different recovery plan. Early lung inflammation can prevent the usual increase to 180 mg.

port_pump.summary: Tablets taken at home; no routine IV line, port or infusion pump is required for brigatinib alone.

anatomy: New cough, breathlessness or fever needs immediate advice, especially during the first week.
Report fainting, slow heartbeat, chest pain or severe headache.
Blood tests check the liver; report jaundice, dark urine or marked illness.
Report unusual thirst, frequent urination or severe abdominal pain.
Report unexplained muscle pain or weakness.
Report new or worsening blurred vision or other changes.
Use sun protection and report severe rash or sun reaction.
Report persistent vomiting or severe diarrhoea; keep fluids up as advised.

questions.q: Why does the dose start lower?
questions.a: The initial seven-day lead-in is part of the brigatinib schedule and helps reduce early pulmonary reactions. Only increase when the team confirms it is appropriate.

questions.q: What if I miss or vomit a dose?
questions.a: Do not take an extra dose. Take the next scheduled dose at the usual time. Contact the team for ongoing vomiting or inability to keep fluids or medicine down.

questions.q: Can I restart my usual tablets after a break?
questions.a: Do not restart or increase brigatinib yourself. A break of 14 days or more for a reason other than a side effect normally needs a new seven-day lead-in before the previously tolerated dose. A break because of a side effect follows a different recovery plan. Early lung inflammation can prevent the usual increase to 180 mg.

questions.q: Does the first-week breathing warning stop after day seven?
questions.a: No. Early reactions are especially important, but lung inflammation can also happen later. Report new or worsening breathing symptoms immediately.

questions.q: How long will I take brigatinib?
questions.a: There is no fixed number of cycles. Your team reviews benefit, side effects, scans and your priorities and agrees whether to continue, change or stop.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide whether tests are safe for treatment?
questions.a: No. The clinical team combines the protocol, symptoms, previous dose changes and organ function before prescribing.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent discussion?
questions.a: Your treatment aim, expected benefit and uncertainty, other options including not proceeding, serious and common harms, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for more time or explanation and reconsider the decision.
